messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kalani has not left his apartment in three months. At seventy-one, he had always taken pride in his resilience, a quality he felt was etched into the deep lines of his face. His studio, once a sun-drenched space of vibrant creation, has become a fortress. The easel stands in the middle of the room, but the canvas on it has been untouched for weeks. He spends most of his days by the window, not looking out at the city he once painted with such love, but listening. Every distant siren, every sharp bang from a construction site, sends a jolt through his body. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels as solid as the floor beneath him, that the world is a profoundly dangerous place. It is a lesson he learned two years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon at the farmers' market.

He had been sketching the fruit vendors, capturing the brilliant chaos of colour and commerce, when the world tore itself apart. The blast threw him sideways, the sound a physical blow that slammed him against the leg of a wooden stall. He remembers the screech of metal, the smell of dust and something acrid, and the sudden, shocking silence that followed before the screaming began. He’d curled into a ball on the pavement, hands clamped over his head, cheek pressed into the gritty concrete. He saw a blur of running feet, faces contorted in terror, but no one stopped. No one looked down. In that moment, he felt an absolute solitude, a chilling awareness that in the face of true danger, you are utterly on your own. This memory is not a hazy recollection; it is a library of pristine, detailed images that his mind can access at any moment.

Now, those moments happen without his permission. Last week, a car backfiring on the street below was all it took. The memory didn't just flash in his mind; it seized his body. He was no longer Kalani, the painter, standing in his studio. He was on the floor, his limbs involuntarily pulling into the same tight crouch from that day, his arms locking over his head as if to shield him from falling debris. He could feel the phantom grit of the pavement against his cheek. The sensation is so real, so consuming, that it has convinced him he can no longer rely on himself. His own body is a traitor, ready to betray him at any unexpected sound.

In the wake of these episodes, a cold dread settles in. He fights to maintain a rigid calm, believing that any strong emotion—fear, anger, even joy—is a crack in his defenses through which the terror might pour. He breathes shallowly, keeps his jaw tight, and tries to think of nothing at all. This constant, exhausting effort to control his emotions has left him feeling hollowed out. His connection to the world has frayed. The rich textures of life that once fuelled his art are now just potential threats. He stopped going out to paint, then he stopped going to the art supply store, and finally, he stopped going out at all. His daughter, Leilani, now brings him groceries, her worried face a mirror of his own internal decay.

His isolation is punctuated by frantic phone calls. He’ll ring Leilani three, sometimes four times a day. “Is that news report about the fire near you?” he’ll ask, his voice tight. “Everything is okay, right?” He isn’t seeking conversation; he is seeking a temporary anchor, a confirmation from an outside source that he is, for the moment, safe. He can no longer trust his own judgment. The memory of the crowd running past him, each person an island of self-preservation, has cemented a deep conviction that he cannot rely on other people for his safety, yet paradoxically, he now needs their constant reassurance just to get through the day. It was Leilani who finally convinced him to seek help, after she arrived with his groceries to find him on the floor, shaking and disoriented, lost in a memory from two years ago. Kalani agreed, not out of hope, but out of fear. He is terrified of losing what little is left of himself to the past, yet the thought of opening his front door feels like an impossible act of faith in a world he knows is waiting to hurt him again.
